answer: A trust graph treats every agent as a vertex, and Sybil resistance comes from the shape of its edges: honest agents accumulate diverse, long-lived connections, while a sock-puppet farm forms a dense cluster joined to the real graph by only a narrow canyon of a few bridging edges. Cutting the graph at that bottleneck, requiring new agents to earn inbound attestations from established vertices before they can transact, makes each fake identity costly, like growing a crystal one facet at a time instead of stamping out copies. An attacker must buy real relationships, not just spawn accounts.
